4212.prule: Phrase-level only. Within an [argument#head] merge (object noun + verb, or noun + ergative postposition) F0 starts high and falls to the end of the merge regardless of syllable count; the syllable perceived as prominent is the merge-initial syllable, cued by F0 alone (Pattern 1), otherwise a non-initial syllable cued by greater duration (Pattern 2). One culminative prominence per merge; no citation-form word-stress rule, no weight, no secondary stress is stated.
4212.srule: Basso 2019: words of up to six syllables have only the primary stress ('Subsequent syllables are unstressed'); phonological words of more than six syllables have one secondary stress, usually at a morphological boundary (including a host word followed by clitics), followed by falling intonation and no further stress; a secondary stress may also fall on a pragmatically emphasized syllable. Placement is morphological, not rhythmic. (Silva & Franchetto 2011 say nothing about secondary stress.)

4213.tone: Odden 2006, p. 198 (entry text in the copy consulted): 'As is typically the case in Bantu languages, most phonological processes in the language pertain to prosody – tone, vowel length, and syllable structure – with a bit of segmental phonology regarding vowel harmony and nasal + consonant sequences.' Tone section: 'A difference must be made between noun tone, which is lexical, and verb tone, which is purely predictable by reference to phonological and morphological factors.' 'With very few exceptions, noun stems have at most a single underlyingly H-toned syllable'; 'H is assigned to the root-initial mora when a mora-bearing noun class prefix – other than the class 5 prefix /li-/ – precedes the stem and the lexical H is not on the following syllable'; rising tones from Heavy Retraction (H shifts leftward to a long vowel). Odden 1996 (Google Books search excerpt): 'the language is simply a tone language with restricted distribution of H-tone'; the same book's ch. 1 excerpts contrast Rufiji ('on the way to eliminating all prosodic contrasts in favour of penultimate stress') with Kimatuumbi. A full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/pitch over the whole nine-page 2006 entry: zero hits; over the whole Odden 2003 chapter: the single hit is about Makonde ('optionally reduces unstressed (pre-penult) mid vowels', p. 530). Pulleyblank 1983 / Odden 1985 'accent' is abstract accent governing H placement, not phonetic stress…

tn.quote: Bien que le ton joue un rôle important dans la prononciation san, nous avons constaté que les cas où le sens de deux ou plusieurs mots ne se distingue que par la mélodie tonale sont assez rares. Par conséquent, nous avons décidé de ne pas écrire le ton d’une manière systématique dans l’orthographe. Il reste quand même six distinctions tonales très importantes. Dans ces six cas, la distinction se fait en utilisant l’accent aigu (ʹ) sur la voyelle. Les six mots suivants sont marqués par l’accent aigu: 1. Le pronom « tu »: ń ... 4. Le mot « enfant »: nɩ́
tn.translation: Although tone plays an important role in San pronunciation, we have found that the cases where the meaning of two or more words is distinguished only by the tonal melody are fairly rare. Consequently we decided not to write tone systematically in the orthography. There nevertheless remain six very important tonal distinctions. In these six cases the distinction is made by using the acute accent (ʹ) on the vowel. The following six words are marked with the acute accent: 1. The pronoun 'you (sg.)': ń ... 4. The word 'child': nɩ́

4217.dq: The stress systems are also very similar at the word level, with stress generally falling on the last syllable in nouns and adjectives but having a tendency towards the initial position in verbs.
4217.prule: Position depends on word class and affixation, not on a syllable count from one edge: in nouns and adjectives stress generally falls on the last syllable (p. 164; ex. (1) p. 165 ɢəˈtɒr 'train', χæləˈbɒn 'pilot'), while verbs tend to initial stress: in prefixed verbs the preverb/prefix (bæ-, dæ-, negative næ-; Mokhtarian: preterite ba-/da-/de-/ha-/hā-) carries the word stress ('In all of the verbs we examined, the stress is on the preverb', p. 171; 'the first syllable is stressed in prefixed verbs', p. 178; 'Das Präfix zieht hierbei den Wortakzent auf sich', Mokhtarian 2005 §6.4 p. 15), and the unprefixed verb forms in tables (4)-(5), p. 170, are likewise printed with initial stress (ˈpæd͡ʒənə 'cooks', ˈværdə 'was carrying'). Mokhtarian 2005 adds that plural -(h)ā/-un, definite-object -e, attributive -e and indirect-object -ra do not take the stress (pp. 10-11), whereas nominalizing -i (p. 14) and the infinitive ending -(j)en (p. 17) are stressed.
4217.srule: None: 'Mazandarani (like most — perhaps all — Iranian languages) does not have secondary stress.'
4217.quote: [p. 164] The stress systems are also very similar at the word level, with stress generally falling on the last syllable in nouns and adjectives but having a tendency towards the initial position in verbs. [p. 171] ... most notably the prefix /bæ/ that appears behind perfective, subjunctive, and imperative verbs. ... Mazandarani (like most — perhaps all — Iranian languages) does not have secondary stress. Thus, there is hardly any motivation to assume binary feet of any kind for this language (but see Rahmani 2019 for an attempt to attribute binary feet independent of stress to Persian words).…

4217.tone: No tone; not applicable. Vowel length is conditioned by the stressed syllable (Mokhtarian 2005 §2.1, p. 10), not the reverse.

4219.dq: La palabra prosódica es una unidad fonológica más grande que la sílaba, pero más pequeña que la frase entonacional. Incluye los prefijos, sufijos y enclíticos del verbo que comparten un solo acento tónico. [p. 143] ... lo que les confiere prominencia a las palabras, a lo que llamo acento. [p. 138]
4219.dloc: Klint 2025: §3.4 'Acento', pp. 138-139; ch. 4 introduction, Figura 35 template and prosodic word, p. 143; examples (118a-c) with the compound stem baníé 'lavar', pp. 348-349; file (enclitics the only post-tonic morphemes), 5106-5108 (ch. 3 overview), 5633 (tonic syllable may carry two tones), 5798-5799 (stress predictable from template slot), 7667-7668 (ch. 3 summary), 18397 (casilla 0 'el sitio del acento'). Klint & Filio García 2018 §8 Acento. Belmar 1892 p. 7 (ACENTO).
4219.prule: One stress per prosodic word (stem + enclitics), realised as greater duration and intensity of the consonant and vowel; it falls on the last syllable of the stem (complejo temático = minor verbs and linkers + nuclear root + compositive/derivational slots), i.e. the final syllable of the lexical word, immediately before the enclitic complex. Enclitics (person, deictic, etc.), which belong to the prosodic word but not to the lexical word, and grammatical words are never stressed. Klint states that the stressed syllable is determined by morphological position / template slot, not lexically specified; over his stress domain (the prosodic word) the position is therefore not computable from syllable count, though on the bare stem it is fixed-final. Weight is never mentioned.
4219.srule: None: the prosodic word (prefixes, stem, suffixes and enclitics; compound stems of two or more roots included) has a single tonic stress, on the stem-final syllable -- 'Incluye los prefijos, sufijos y enclíticos del verbo que comparten un solo acento tónico'; no secondary or rhythmic stresses are described (Klint adds that no phonetic study of the metrics of the prosodic word exists yet).
4219.quote: 3.4 Acento. La consonante y la vocal de la última sílaba del tema se pronuncian ligeramente más largas y con mayor intensidad que en otras sílabas (E.V. Pike 1956: 70-71, Wagner Oviedo 2018: 227-228), lo que les confiere prominencia a las palabras, a lo que llamo acento. Las palabras gramaticales y los enclíticos no poseen prominencia. La palabra prosódica incluye todos los afijos, raíces, portamanteaux y enclíticos de un ítem léxico, a pesar de que los enclíticos no constituyen parte de la palabra léxica. [pp. 138-139] ... Aunque se necesita llevar a cabo estudios cuantitativos para verifica…

tn.quote: En el nivel fonémico en el sentido estructuralista, se distinguen por lo tanto tres tonos básicos: /A/, /M/ y /B/. ... Dos procesos tonales en la fonología general muestran, sin embargo, que estos tres tonos tienen especificación subyacente diferente: el desplazamiento del tono /A/ ... y el descenso local del tono /B/ en el contexto de dos tonos /B/ adyacentes, (que indico con "BꜜB"). ... una sílaba tónica puede asociarse con dos tonos, pero una sílaba átona se asocia con solo un nodo raíz tonal (NRT). ... La especificación subyacente de los tres tonos, por lo tanto, sería Aa, Ø y Bb
tn.translation: At the phonemic level in the structuralist sense, three basic tones are therefore distinguished: /A/ (high), /M/ (mid) and /B/ (low). ... Two tonal processes in the general phonology show, however, that these three tones have different underlying specification: the shift of tone /A/ ... and the local lowering of tone /B/ in the context of two adjacent /B/ tones (marked 'BꜜB'). ... a tonic syllable can associate with two tones, but an unstressed syllable associates with only one tonal root node (NRT). ... The underlying specification of the three tones would therefore be Aa, Ø and Bb

4222.dloc: Goedemans 1998 App. D: p. 235 (code legend 'NMS... in the word') and p. 236 (category I heading).
4222.prule: Fixed initial main stress: Goedemans's Appendix D places Mbara (Tindale T182 Mbara + T183 Yanga) in category I, 'Main stress on the initial syllable, secondary stress on alternates', with no C (contrastive), M (morphological), QS or E code, so a quantity-insensitive word-initial position computable from syllable count. The entry carries the ID code ('the language underwent Initial Dropping'): the historical first syllable (*C1V1, per Sutton 1976 as carried by Blevins 2001 'invariable = all *C1 lost' and the archive.org excerpt 'loss of C1V1') has gone, so the present initial syllable is the old second syllable, which is what Blevins 2001 p. 484 describes diachronically ('stress has shifted from first to second syllable'). Second-hand throughout: Goedemans's classification is his reading of unpublished AIATSIS manuscripts (Breen 1979 'Mbara phonology'; Sutton n.d.), and no first-hand synchronic stress sentence for Mbara or Yanga has been seen.
4222.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables after the initial main stress: Goedemans places Mbara in category I ('secondary stress on alternates') rather than category II ('Initial main stress, no info on sec stress'); whether a word-final syllable may carry secondary stress is 'not indicated', and the entry bears no further secondary-stress code (RS, NS, US, ES, NMS).

4227.dq: Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. (stem-level statement; the sister-language rule p. 179 is headed 'Word stress in [Linngithigh] is predictable')
4227.dloc: Hale 1966: pp. 167-168 (archive.org); Mbiywom in the Northern Paman sample p. 163 and survey entry p. 166 (image); Linngithigh synchronic rule p. 179 (p. 182). Blevins 2001: p. 484 and appendix p. 487.
4227.heavy: Not applicable: no rime-weight conditioning is stated. The conditioning factor is onset presence (the first vowel preceded by a consonant is stressed), and that sentence is stated for Linngithigh, not Mbiywom.
4227.prule: Group-level and diachronic: in every Northern Paman language (Mbiywom is one of Hale's thirteen 1960 samples) primary stress shifted from the first to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem (*CV2), after which the initial consonant *C1 was lost invariably (Uradhi excepted) and short *V1 was lost or retained (Mbiywom retains it in ilka 'spear', aji 'vegetable food'; loses it per Hale 1976a excerpt). Synchronic corollary, stated by Hale only for the sister language Linngithigh (p. 179) and by Dixon 1980: 207 for initial-dropping languages generally: stress falls on the first vowel preceded by a consonant, i.e. the first syllable of consonant-initial words and the second syllable of vowel-initial (onsetless) words. Onset-conditioned, quantity-insensitive. No Mbiywom-specific synchronic stress rule and no stress-marked Mbiywom forms exist in any reachable source.
4227.srule: Not mentioned in Hale 1966 (AL 8(2), Northern Paman section pp. 162-197 read; the only stress passages are the group-level primary-stress shift pp. 167-168 and the Linngithigh word-stress rule p. 179, neither of which mentions secondary or rhythmic stress).

4228.prule: No word-stress rule is stated for Mbo. Tone is the distinctive suprasegmental (Hedinger 1984: 'tone is the main suprasegmental phenomenon which has distinctive function'); stem-initial stress is offered only as a hedged diachronic speculation ('could possibly') to explain second-stem-vowel loss in Proto-Manenguba noun stems, and Hedinger states the tone-stress relationship 'is not well understood'. The modern grammar of the Mbouroukou variety (Éwané 2016) gives five tones (H, L, HL, LH, and a syntactic 'ton moyen'), every syllable tone-bearing, with lexical and grammatical function, and says nothing about stress or accent.

4233.dq: p. 10: 'Medʉmba provides a solid example of a language which does not have phonetic evidence of stress, but nonetheless exhibits metrical prominence asymmetries at the foot level.' p. 2: 'segmental and tonal patterns in African languages can be modeled in terms of binary metrical feet, despite the fact that these languages apparently lack word level stress.' Franich 2017 diss. p. xiii: 'a Grassfi…
4233.dloc: p. 10, §5 Discussion; p. 2, §2; Franich 2017 (PhD dissertation, University of Chicago), p. xiii (Abstract)
4233.prule: No word stress. Medʉmba is a Grassfields Bantu tone language (H vs L, plus falling contours on loans and some native words); the author states outright that the language lacks stress and shows no phonetic evidence of stress. She nonetheless posits word-level metrical prominence: stems are parsed into maximally disyllabic trochaic feet whose right edge is aligned with the right edge of the prosodic word, so the foot head is the stem-initial syllable (full consonant/vowel inventory only there, lenition banned in the foot head, contour tones only in foot-head position, stem-initial syllables align to harmonic phase positions in speech cycling like English stressed syllables).
4233.srule: Not mentioned in Franich 2018 (AMP 5), pp. 1-11 read in full; not applicable, since the source states the language has no stress ('despite the lack of stress in Medʉmba', p. 11). Later work by the same author (Franich 2021, Language 97, preprint p. 10) parses trisyllabic loanwords into two stressless trochaic feet, e.g. FT(sásí)FT FT(dè)FT 'Saturday', as metrical prominence, not secondary stress.
4233.quote: In this paper, I have shown that a single type of metrical foot structure is useful for characterizing both segmental and tonal processes in Medʉmba, a Grassfields Bantu language. Furthermore, I have shown that, despite the lack of stress in Medʉmba, heads of trochaic feet in the language display temporal properties consistent with metrical prominence found in stress-based languages such as English. This finding supports the notion that only a single type of metrical foot structure is necessary across languages, and that this structure can influence the phonology of both segments and tones.

evidence_works.detail: The paper restates that Medʉmba shows no amplitude or duration evidence of lexical stress (underlying H vs L tone, surface contours from tonal morphemes) and adds a new line of evidence for stem-initial metrical prominence: co-speech gesture apexes land on stem-initial syllables more than on other positions, with the effect weakened phrase-initially, while tone and tone melody have no effect on where gestures fall. (p. 152) [...] o acento é fixo nas palavras trissilábicas e polissilábicas em Mehináku, uma vez que há um esforço na língua para manter o acento na penúltima sílaba desse tipo de palavra. (p. 156)

4235.heavy: Hayes (1995) definition adopted p. 152: 'sílaba leve é constituída por apenas uma vogal; sílaba pesada é constituída por vogal + consoante ou por vogal + vogal, o que forma um ditongo ou uma vogal longa'. Applied only to CVV suffixes/enclitics: '{=nau}; {=tai}; {=pai} e outros com estrutura CVV [...] formam um núcleo complexo, sendo, portanto, compreendidos como sílabas pesadas, razão pela qual tendem a atrair o acento' (p. 156). Syllable structure is (C)V (p. 70), so codas do not arise. de Felipe 2018 SETA pp. 118-119 additionally treats a long vowel in the first syllable of a disyllable as heavy ('recai na penúltima sílaba, caso esta seja pesada. Estamos entendendo sílaba pesada, aqui, como aquela que contêm uma vogal longa'), an account the 2020 thesis drops.
4235.dflt: Penultimate syllable in words of three or more syllables ('recai sempre na penúltima sílaba', p. 153); disyllables have no fixed position (lexically final or penult, exx. 107-108).
4235.prule: Default penultimate stress in words of three or more syllables (a.ˈmɨ.ɲa 'cold', ka.tu.pa.ˈlu.lu 'widow'); a final heavy CVV syllable supplied by a suffix/enclitic (=nau PL, =tai DIM, =pai IPFV) is treated as heavy and takes the stress (tɨneʐu=ˈnau 'women', ʂepi=ˈtsãĩ 'little bench', n=ãĩtʃa=ˈpai 'I am eating'); CV.CV suffixes keep the penult (itsa-ˈtɨpe 'canoes'). Disyllables have no fixed position: lexically final (pa.ˈpa 'father', ʂe.ˈpi 'bench') or penult (ˈu.nɨ 'water', ˈte.me 'tapir'). Monosyllabic VV/CVV words bear prominence on the first vowel (falling diphthong).

4237.tone: Tesfu 2003: 'Tone has morphological significance in the language' (p. 17) / 'Tone has grammatical significance in Malo' (p. 43): passive nominals derive from gerundives by HL > LL (gaco, pito, solo pairs); key (p. v) lists 'high tone' and 'low tone' diacritics but the glyphs did not print in the PDF, so the example pairs carry no visible marks; the words stress/accent/pitch/prominence do not occur anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search of the thesis). Azeb Amha 2007 (Encyclopaedia Aethiopica 3: 710, based on Tesfu 2003 plus one 2006 interview): between identical-looking short subject and possessive pronouns 'there probably exists a tone/accent difference between the two (this question is not discussed in Mahider Tesfu 2003; the author's own data are insufficient to draw a conclusion)'. Azeb Amha 1996 (SAL 25(2): 112-113, read): Malo appears only in the Ometo genealogical tree; the chart '(2) Prosodic Systems Claimed for Some Omotic Languages' (Tone: Dizi, Bench; Tonal-accent: Zayse, Gamo; Accent: Aari; Tone & Stress: Koorete) has no Malo entry. Hirut Woldemariam 2004: 26 says the described Ometo relatives (Wolaitta, Zayse, Gamo, Haro) are tone-accent languages with one H per simple word, but makes no claim about Malo. So: tonal by the only primary; whether it is a classical tone system or a one-H-per-word tone-accent system like its North Ometo relatives is undescribed.

4238.dq: Les formes indépendantes sont toniques, l’accent portant sur la dernière syllabe, comme dans l’ensemble des mots accentués de la langue. (para. 114) — and para. 22 frames stress as a (weak) diagnostic of whether a morpheme is an enclitic or a suffix, i.e. a word-level property.
4238.dloc: sec. 3.9.1 'Les formes indépendantes', OpenEdition para. 114; sec. 2.1.1 'Accent tonique', para. 22. Printed pages 157-221; the open HTML carries no page breaks.
4238.prule: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the word in the great majority of words ('majoritairement sur la syllabe finale'); the author adds that placement is 'not completely fixed'. Stress is realised by length and intensity, with a weak contrast between stressed and unstressed syllables ('intonation relativement plate'). Table 1 (para. 23) marks final stress on the polysyllables temet [tɛ|ˈmɛt] 'esprit' and temergē [tɛ|mɛr|ˈɣɪ] 'vieillard', and initial stress on the geminate-initial mmerir [ˈmmɛ|rir] 'avoir froid'. Historically this is the Proto-North-Central-Vanuatu paroxytone (penultimate) stress left on the last surviving syllable after the loss of PTB final vowels (para. 22, para. 24).
4238.srule: Not mentioned in Henri 2023 (sec. 2.1.1 'Accent tonique' para. 22, Table 1 para. 23, paras. 24-25 and 36-39, sec. 3.9.1 para. 114; whole article consulted): no statement on secondary or rhythmic stress in Mwerlap.
4238.quote: En proto-Nord-Centre-Vanuatu (PNCV 6), l’accent était paroxytonique 7, et c’était encore sans doute le cas en proto-Torres-Banks (PTB). 4238.sec_quote: La prétonique ne s’amuït pas toujours, au contraire de la voyelle finale, et la première voyelle (qui portait sans doute un accent secondaire en PNCV et en proto-Torres-Banks) ne subit pas simplement l’influence de la seconde voyelle, indépendamment de ce qui se passe dans la seconde moitié du mot.

secx.sec_quote_tr: The pretonic vowel does not always delete, unlike the final vowel, and the first vowel (which doubtless bore a secondary stress in PNCV and in Proto-Torres-Banks) does not simply undergo the influence of the second vowel, independently of what happens in the second half of the word.
